subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Uses of exothermic and endothermic changes

questions.q: An exothermic reaction is one that:
options: Transfers energy to the surroundings, usually raising the temperature
Takes in energy from the surroundings, lowering the temperature
Neither takes in nor gives out energy
questions.explain: Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings usually rises.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of an endothermic process?
options: Neutralising an acid with an alkali
questions.explain: Thermal decomposition takes in energy (endothermic). Combustion, neutralisation and crystallisation are exothermic.

questions.q: In an endothermic reaction, the temperature of the surroundings will:
questions.explain: Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings, so the surroundings cool down (temperature falls).

questions.lo: Uses of exothermic and endothermic changes
questions.q: A sports injury cold pack works by which type of reaction?
options: Endothermic, so it takes in heat and feels cold
questions.explain: Cold packs use an endothermic process (e.g. dissolving ammonium nitrate) that absorbs heat, making the pack feel cold.

questions.lo: Uses of exothermic and endothermic changes
questions.q: Self-heating cans and hand warmers make use of:
questions.explain: Hand warmers and self-heating cans rely on exothermic reactions that transfer heat energy to the surroundings.

questions.q: On a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction, the products are:
options: At the same energy level as the reactants
At a higher energy level than the reactants
At a lower energy level than the reactants
questions.explain: In an exothermic reaction, energy is released, so the products sit at a lower energy than the reactants.

questions.q: On a reaction profile for an endothermic reaction, the products are:
options: At the same energy as the activation energy peak
At a lower energy level than the reactants
At a higher energy level than the reactants
questions.explain: Endothermic reactions absorb energy, so the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants.

questions.q: The activation energy of a reaction is:
options: The total energy of the products
The energy released when bonds form
The minimum energy that colliding particles must have to react
The energy stored in the reactants only
questions.explain: Activation energy is the minimum energy that reacting particles must have for a successful collision to occur.

questions.q: On a reaction profile, the activation energy is shown by:
options: The height from the reactants up to the top of the curve
The difference in height between reactants and products
The height of the products above zero
questions.explain: Activation energy is the energy gap from the reactant level up to the peak of the reaction profile.

questions.q: During a chemical reaction, energy is:
options: Released to break bonds and taken in when new bonds form
Taken in to break bonds and released when new bonds form
questions.explain: Breaking bonds is endothermic (absorbs energy); making bonds is exothermic (releases energy).

questions.q: A reaction absorbs 1500 kJ breaking bonds and releases 1650 kJ forming bonds. The overall energy change is:
questions.explain: Energy change = energy in - energy out = 1500 - 1650 = -150 kJ. Negative means exothermic (more released than absorbed).

questions.q: If breaking bonds requires more energy than is released making bonds, the reaction is:
questions.explain: When more energy is absorbed (breaking) than released (making), the overall change is positive, so the reaction is endothermic.

questions.q: A simple cell produces a voltage when:
options: Two different metals are connected in an electrolyte
The metals are placed in pure water
questions.explain: A cell needs two different metals (with different reactivities) in an electrolyte; the bigger the reactivity difference, the larger the voltage.

questions.q: What determines the size of the voltage produced by a simple cell?
options: The temperature of the room only
The difference in reactivity of the two metals used
questions.explain: The greater the difference in reactivity between the two metal electrodes, the greater the voltage of the cell.

questions.q: Why do non-rechargeable cells eventually stop producing electricity?
options: One of the reactants is used up and the reaction cannot be reversed
They run out of electrons permanently made in the factory
questions.explain: In non-rechargeable cells the reaction stops once a reactant is used up, and it cannot be reversed by recharging.

questions.q: A rechargeable battery can be recharged because:
options: It never runs out of reactants
It generates new metal each time
The chemical reactions can be reversed by passing a current through it
questions.explain: Rechargeable cells work because the chemical reactions can be reversed when an external current is applied, reforming the reactants.

questions.q: In a hydrogen fuel cell, the overall reaction produces:
questions.explain: A hydrogen fuel cell reacts hydrogen with oxygen to produce water only, releasing energy as electricity.

questions.q: What is oxidised at the negative electrode of a hydrogen fuel cell?
questions.explain: At the negative electrode, hydrogen loses electrons (is oxidised): 2H2 -> 4H+ + 4e-.

questions.q: One advantage of a hydrogen fuel cell over a rechargeable battery is that fuel cells:
options: Store more energy per kilogram in all cases
Never need a supply of fuel
Do not need recharging and produce only water as waste
questions.explain: Fuel cells keep working while hydrogen is supplied (no recharging needed) and their only product is water, which is clean.

questions.q: A disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cells is that:
options: They contain toxic heavy metals like lead
They release large amounts of carbon dioxide
Hydrogen is difficult and expensive to store and transport safely
questions.explain: Hydrogen is a flammable gas that is hard to store and transport safely, which is a key drawback of fuel cells.
